items.text: Depression often takes the want. Autistic burnout often takes the can. The interest is still there — you just can't reach it. These aren't the same thing, and they don't respond the same way.
items.rationale: The lost-want vs. lost-can distinction is the sharpest, most defensible version of this angle — it names a recognisable felt experience without overstating the clinical picture or making any treatment claim.

items.text: Remote work was an accommodation many neurodivergent workers never had to ask for. RTO mandates are removing it. That's not a perk rolling back — that's an access issue.
items.rationale: Connects a live structural story to a plain reframe: what passed as a workplace perk was doing disability-access work all along. Clean and direct — no outrage framing required.

items.text: AuDHD: the autistic nervous system regulates through sameness. The ADHD nervous system needs novelty. Both live in you. So 'just rest' can soothe one system while actively destabilising the other.
items.rationale: Names the AuDHD internal conflict with mechanical precision — not 'it's complicated' but exactly why the two systems conflict. The colon-and-short-sentence structure lets the idea land in layers.

items.text: Getting a late autism diagnosis and feeling both relieved and devastated isn't a contradiction. It's rarely named — and most people aren't warned about the grief. You're allowed to feel both.
items.rationale: Holds the relief-grief paradox without resolving it. The permission at the end lands because the middle sentence has already confirmed this is common, not a failure of gratitude.

items.text: Breathing exercises can't fix an environment that attacks your nervous system all day. Chronic dysregulation is often structural — unmet sensory needs, hostile environments, insufficient support. That's not a regulation skill problem.
items.rationale: Takes the most saturated corner of neurodivergent content (regulation tips) and redirects: the problem isn't a skill deficit, it's structural. Draws on Charlie Wilding's framing, tightened.

items.text: 'Pathological Demand Avoidance' locates the problem in the person. 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy' names what's actually happening: a nervous system responding to felt threat. Same experience. Completely different question.
items.rationale: The two names side by side do the entire work. Readers who already know PDA feel the shift immediately; readers who don't get a precise introduction without jargon overhead.

items.text: If therapy keeps not working and nobody can explain why — autistic burnout is worth knowing about. It looks like depression from the outside. It isn't the same thing inside.
items.rationale: Opens on a felt experience and closes with a factual pointer rather than advice. Validates confusion and offers a direction to look without directing treatment decisions.
items.sensitivity_flag: Mild: pairing 'therapy not working' with burnout framing edges toward advisory territory. No treatment recommendation is made, but worth a second read before posting.

items.text: Saying no to the loud venue, the last-minute plan change, the overloaded schedule — for many autistic people that's not rigidity. That's nervous-system care. Calling it a personality flaw misses what's actually happening.
items.rationale: Takes something long pathologised ('inflexibility') and gives it a compassionate functional explanation. The concrete examples carry the reframe so the closing line doesn't have to labour it.

items.text: Diagnosis doesn't hand you an unmasked self. Many late-diagnosed autistic people spend years knowing they've been masking without yet knowing who they are underneath. That liminal place is real. You don't have to rush through it.
items.rationale: Fills the gap in post-diagnosis content: most posts cover the relief; this one names the long disorienting middle. High recognition for people months or years past diagnosis who feel like they 'should' feel better by now.

items.text: Should workplace accommodations require a formal diagnosis to access? Or should quiet spaces, flexible routines, and written instructions just be... how workplaces work? What does the community actually want here?
items.rationale: Opens a genuine debate rather than supplying an answer. The community has real disagreements — universal design versus explicitly naming specific needs — and surfacing the tension invites more honest conversation than pre-resolving it.

items.text: The planner drawer. Every neurodivergent person knows it — bought with optimism, abandoned with shame. The tool didn't fail. It was built for a brain that isn't yours.
items.rationale: One concrete image carries the entire reframe. Recognition lands before the point is made, so the final line arrives on a reader who already feels seen rather than lectured.

items.text: The diagnosis doesn't change what happened. It changes what it meant. That realisation is both a relief and a weight. You're allowed to hold both at once.
items.rationale: Draws directly on the HeyASD framing and extends it one beat to keep the paradox open rather than resolve it. Short and final-sounding — designed to cut through rather than develop.
